title: Efficiency Matters and Perfection is a Mirage: Updates to the Article of the Week for 2021-2022
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart explains two changes he made to Kelly Gallagher's Article of the Week (AOW) strategy during the pivot to 1:1 technology in COVID-era teaching, and generalizes the reasoning behind them. First, he stopped converting each week's article into a PDF or Google Doc and started linking directly within the LMS, cutting his own prep friction. Second, going 1:1 lowered the friction of sharing articles enough that he began using short articles more than once a week, especially as daily warm-ups sourced from newsletters like Morning Brew. He walks through the resulting pros (easier incidental knowledge-building, faster sourcing, remote-friendly access) and cons (browser distraction, occasional paywalls), landing on the practical maxim that anchors the piece: efficiency matters and perfection is a mirage. He closes by reminding readers that sharing an article isn't an endorsement and that teachers remain responsible for vetting what they assign.
points: Stuart's practical decision rule for curricular tools: when a workflow change (like linking instead of formatting PDFs) removes friction without sacrificing the underlying learning goal, take it -- 'efficiency matters and perfection is a mirage.'
Going 1:1 didn't just change format, it changed frequency and use case: he moved from a weekly AOW ritual to using short articles as near-daily warm-ups, increasing incidental knowledge-building.
He names the real tradeoff of digital-first sourcing explicitly: browser distraction and periodic paywalls versus faster, lower-friction access to timely content.

He draws an explicit ethical line around curation: sharing an article is not an endorsement, and teachers are responsible for knowing their community, administrators, and students well enough to vet what they assign.
quotes: Since all my students had computers and some of them were remote or quarantining at any given time, I found the process of converting each week's article into a PDF or Google Doc needlessly cumbersome.
Because I'm eager for my students to learn as much as they can — and because 1:1 decreased the friction of sharing articles with my students — I started using articles more than 1x/week.

When I found an interesting article that related to any of our burning questions of the year or current topics of interest in our curriculum, I could easily incorporate it into my lessons — no need to copy/paste/format/print/etc.

I still dislike the added distraction that a computer's web browser presents — for children and for adults. Reading articles on a news website inevitably means exposure to advertisements and temptations to Ctl+T your way into a (likely defocusing) new tab/game/experience.

So, like normal, ain't no silver bullets and no perfect scenarios. However, for me the life-enhancing, democratizing and emancipating power of a knowledge-rich curricula outweighs the drawbacks of added sources of distraction and periodically annoying paywalls.
As always, remember that we're each responsible for the articles we share with our students. Know your setting, know your community, know your administrators.
Know what you're after: student long-term flourishing via optimized mastery outcomes without sacrificing your life on the altar of professional success. Pursue this doggedly.
